hook.text: Bacteria carry molecular scissors that cut invading virus DNA — scientists borrowed them for genetic engineering.

buildup.text: Restriction enzymes recognize specific DNA sequences, usually 4 to 8 letters long, and cut precisely.

discovery.text: EcoRI cuts at GAATTC — leaving sticky ends that can join with any other DNA cut by the same enzyme.

twist.text: Over 4,000 restriction enzymes are known — each cuts a different sequence, giving engineers a vast toolkit.

climax.text: Werner Arber, Daniel Nathans, and Hamilton Smith won the 1978 Nobel Prize for discovering these molecular scissors.

punchline.text: Bacteria made the scissors — humans learned to cut with them.

quiz.question: What are sticky ends in restriction enzyme cuts?
options: Enzymes that remain attached to DNA after cutting
Single-stranded DNA overhangs that can pair with complementary cuts
Damaged DNA ends that cannot be repaired

details.summary: Restriction enzymes are bacterial proteins that cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, serving as molecular scissors that enabled the birth of genetic engineering. Discovered in the 1970s, they remain essential tools for cloning, mapping, and analyzing DNA in molecular biology laboratories.
details.whyItMatters: Restriction enzymes launched the era of recombinant DNA technology. Their discovery earned the 1978 Nobel Prize and made it possible to cut, paste, and recombine DNA from any organism, creating the foundation for all genetic engineering that
takeaways: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific short recognition sequences
They create sticky or blunt ends enabling DNA fragment joining with ligase
Their discovery earned the 1978 Nobel Prize and launched genetic engineering

faq.question: Why do bacteria naturally produce restriction enzymes?
faq.answer: Restriction enzymes are part of the bacterial restriction-modification immune system. They cut foreign DNA from invading phages at specific sequences while the bacterium's own DNA is protected by methylation at those same sequences. This defense system predates CRISPR immunity.

faq.question: Are restriction enzymes still relevant now that CRISPR exists?
faq.answer: Yes. Restriction enzymes remain essential for routine molecular cloning, DNA mapping, quality control of constructs, and many diagnostic applications. They are simpler and cheaper than CRISPR for basic cut-and-paste operations.
